newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan calms hog farmers to avert Taipei protest.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan calms hog farmers to avert Taipei protest.

text.p: Farm officials have defused a planned mass protest by angry Taiwan hog breeders by pledging to consider new financial aid to help them weather a foot and mouth disease outbreak, breeders said on Friday.
"The Council of Agriculture officials agreed to meet with us to discuss the compensation plan," an spokesman for the Republic of China Swine Association told Reuters by telephone.
Farm council vice chairman Ling Shiang-nung would meet pig farmers on Friday to discuss ways of financing an islandwide hog slaughter and other financial assistance, the spokesman said.
The farm council already has proposed to compensate breeders T$2,400 for each slaughtered pig and T$350 for each piglet.
The swine association says that is not enough, demanding T$3,000 per pig, the spokesman said.
The association had planned to bring the dispute to the capital's streets on Friday with a mass protest by farmers.

The protest was called off after council officials warned that bringing thousands of farmers to Taipei would risk spreading the highly contagious pig foot and mouth disease virus, which is airborne and can be tranmitted by humans.
"We realised that it would be dangerous to have pig farmers from infected areas gather at one place," the spokesman said.

The fast-moving epidemic was found to have infected 716 pig breeding farms as of late on Wednesday, up from just nine on the day the epidemic was announced, March 20, and double the number reported on Monday.

Experts backed by soldiers continued a mass slaughter of all pigs, even healthy ones, at farms plagued by the scourge, with agriculture officials reporting on Wednesday that over 666,000 diseased and healthy pigs were being destroyed.
Industry sources quoted by the ruling Nationalist Party have estimated that about 15 percent of Taiwan's 11 million swine -- or 1.6 million animals -- would be affected directly.
Millions of vaccine doses airlifted to Taiwan this week were being distributed in hopes of checking the contagion's spread, with healthy hogs and other livestock slated for vaccination.
The farm council banned all pork exports after confirming the outbreak on March 20, when the virus had been detected in nine of the island's 25,000 hog breeding farms.

Across the island, masked soldiers in plastic suits have wielded electric prods to stun pigs, then used huge earth movers to dump them into incinerators or giant pits -- often with the pigs still gasping for air.
